text:
*Interview with Dr Casimir Vauthier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Thank you for waiting, Doctor. Sit wherever you are comfortable. You have known the family a long time.

DR VAUTHIER: Thirty years, Inspector. I have been Aurèle's physician and, I hope, his friend, though with Aurèle the two were not always the same thing. You will forgive me if I light a cigar. I have wanted one since your men arrived, and my hands are not behaving.

MATTHEY: Please. Tell me about the dinner.

DR VAUTHIER: Aurèle did what he does every year. When the temple bell struck nine, he had us all put our watches on the cloth, and he went down the table like a jeweller over a stone. He tells you what is wrong with your watch, and you go away a little humbled. Mine was two minutes ahead of the bell. I said I kept it so for the sake of my patients. He said it was the only honest thing about it.

MATTHEY: And after dinner?

DR VAUTHIER: Odile and I played piquet in the salon. Odile plays better than I do, and she knows it, and she is kind enough to let me believe otherwise until the last hand. We played until a quarter to eleven by my watch. Then I went out to the hall to fetch my cigar case from my coat. Madame began to play the piano as I went out. She was playing Chopin. She plays Chopin when she has nothing to say, which is seldom. She stopped when I came back.

MATTHEY: You sat down again.

DR VAUTHIER: I did, and the hall clock struck eleven a moment after I sat down again. It is the old Morbier. It strikes the hours from its own face, and no one in this house has ever argued with it.

MATTHEY: You are sure of the clock.

DR VAUTHIER: Inspector, I have heard that clock for thirty years. I am not likely to mistake it now.

MATTHEY: Let us come to the atelier. What did you know of Aurèle's work?

DR VAUTHIER: Very little, and I was rather proud of my ignorance. He talked about the repeater as other men talk about their wives. He would press the slide for me across this table, the low notes and then the doubled quarters, and look at me as though I had failed an examination.

MATTHEY: You have seen the body.

DR VAUTHIER: I will answer what I can and no more. A blow to the back of the head. Death would have been very quick. I should think he knew nothing of it, and I hope that is true, for Odile's sake, because she will want it to be true. I will not give you an hour, Inspector. Medicine is less exact than a watch, whatever Aurèle believed.

MATTHEY: The regulator in the atelier has stopped.

DR VAUTHIER: Has it? Then it stopped with its master. I know that is sentimental. I am a doctor, and I am allowed one sentiment, and I have just used it.

MATTHEY: You attended the family before this, I think.

DR VAUTHIER: Jules Monnier, Aurèle's brother, in his last illness, in 1889. Félix's father. I sat with him more than I should have, because I liked him. Jules was a better man than Aurèle and never half so clever with a watch. When I came to this house afterwards, I think it was a comfort to Odile, and I have tried to go on being one.

MATTHEY: And Madame Monnier?

DR VAUTHIER: Odile is the most exact woman I know. She does not cry in front of people, and she would not thank you for asking whether she did. Thirty years of marriage wear a thing smooth. She loved him as one loves a well-made object that was never once allowed to be careless.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Doctor. That will be all for now.

DR VAUTHIER: *De mortuis nil nisi bonum*, Inspector. I shall try. It is harder than the Romans supposed.
